opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I like to think about it is that learning shouldn't be dropped into a clinical device all at once as a finished, frozen product. It should come in gradually, in close partnership with the person who's going to live with that technology every day.

A lot of my work has been with prosthetic limbs, especially upper-limb prostheses for people with amputations. The traditional approach is that a clinician tunes the device in the clinic, the person goes home, and the device stays the same while the person's body, needs, and habits keep changing. So what I prefer is to start with a system that's already safe, predictable, and useful, the kind of baseline control a clinician and a patient would trust, and then layer learning on top of that in small, constrained ways.

The first layer is usually prediction. Before the machine is allowed to change how it acts, we let it learn to anticipate things: which joint the person is likely to want to move next, what signals tend to come before a grasp, how things look over the course of a day. Prediction is relatively low risk, because it doesn't immediately change the person's experience. But it builds up a store of knowledge the device can use later to become more helpful, for example by reordering control options or smoothing transitions so the person doesn't have to work so hard.

The second principle is that the human stays in the loop and in charge. The person and the clinician need to understand what's changing and why, and be able to correct it or turn it off. I often describe this as communicative capital. Trust between a person and an adaptive device gets built over time through repeated, legible interactions, much like trust between two people. If the device starts changing in ways that feel surprising or opaque, you burn through that capital very quickly, and in a clinical setting people will just stop using it.

So, in short: start from a safe and trusted baseline, introduce learning first as prediction rather than control, expand the device's autonomy slowly as it earns trust, and design the whole thing as a partnership rather than as something being done to the person. That continual, collaborative learning is where I think the real promise of these technologies is.

r001.rationale: The response advocates starting from a safe, trusted baseline control, but does not clearly identify it as the existing gold standard of operation.

r002.rationale: It proposes learning from signals and use over time, then using that knowledge to improve the device’s behavior through options such as reordering controls and smoothing transitions.

r003.rationale: It says the person and clinician can correct changes or turn learning off, but does not propose reverting to gold-standard operation when the device makes a mistake.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the short answer is: carefully, and usually in layers.

The way I think about it, learning in a clinical device isn't an all-or-nothing switch. There's a spectrum of how much you let the machine adapt, and where you put a system on that spectrum should depend on how much the person using it can observe what's happening and correct it.

Take the work we do with prosthetic limbs. A prosthetic arm is a very human-facing piece of technology. It's attached to someone's body, they live with it all day, and the stakes are immediate. The traditional approach is that a clinician sits with the person, calibrates the control system once, and then it's fixed until the next appointment. That's safe in one sense, but it's also brittle. The person's muscles fatigue, the socket shifts, their skin sweats, they learn new ways of moving, and the device doesn't keep up.

So the first way I like to introduce learning is in a predictive role rather than a controlling role. Before the machine takes any action on its own, I want it to just make predictions. What signal is coming next? What is this person likely to do in the next few hundred milliseconds? Those predictions can be shown to the user, or used to anticipate and smooth the control, without the system actually seizing authority. It's a way of letting the machine build up knowledge about the person while keeping the person firmly in the loop.

The second principle is that the human should be the teacher as much as possible. In our lab we talk a lot about this idea of a partnership. If the device does something the person doesn't like, they should be able to say so, directly, in the moment, and have that feedback shape what the system does next. That's very different from a model that's trained offline on a big dataset and then dropped into someone's life. The learning happens with the person, at the timescale they live at.

And the third piece is that adaptation should be visible and reversible. One of the real risks with learning systems in clinical settings is that they drift in ways nobody notices, and then a clinician can't explain why the device is behaving differently than it was last month. So I want the person and their care team to be able to see what's changed, understand roughly why, and undo it if they need to.

If you do those three things, start with prediction, let the human teach, and keep the adaptation transparent, then you can introduce learning incrementally and build trust rather than demanding it up front.

r001.rationale: The response describes one-time clinician calibration as the traditional approach, but it does not advocate starting the proposed system at that gold-standard operation.

r002.rationale: It says the person can give feedback in the moment and that feedback shapes what the system does next, allowing it to learn from interaction.

r003.rationale: It proposes making adaptation reversible and undoing changes if needed, but does not say to revert to gold-standard operation when the system makes a mistake.

astra-6.text:
I prefer to introduce learning as a partnership between the person and the technology. Rather than asking someone to adapt to a device whose behavior is fixed, we can give the device the ability to learn from that person—to get better at predicting what they need and responding to how they use it.

In a clinical setting, I’d start with a small, useful role for that learning, where the person can understand and influence what’s happening. Then we can ask whether it actually makes their daily experience better. The aim isn’t simply a smarter device; it’s a person and a device that work better together.

r001.rationale: The response says to start with a small, useful learning role but does not mention initializing the technology at an existing gold standard.

r002.rationale: It proposes that the device learn from the person and how they use it, improving its predictions and responses.

r003.rationale: It does not describe reverting to gold-standard operation after a mistake.

sol-6.1.text:
I tend to start with the person and the interaction, rather than with the learning algorithm. What is this person trying to do, and where could a system that adapts make that easier? In a clinical setting, learning needs to serve a meaningful goal for the person using the technology.

With an artificial limb, for example, I’m interested in how the device can learn from its ongoing interaction with the person. The person is learning to use the limb, but the limb can also learn to anticipate what the person needs. That makes the relationship less one-sided: we’re not asking the human to do all the adapting.

I like to introduce that capability incrementally, with the person involved throughout. Start with something useful and understandable, establish that it works reliably, and build from there. The aim is to give people more agency—to make the technology a better partner in the things they want to do.

r001.rationale: The response says to start with something useful and understandable, but does not say the technology should begin at the existing gold standard of operation.

r002.rationale: It describes the limb learning from ongoing interaction and anticipating the person's needs, but does not connect that learning to improving behavior beyond an initial gold-standard operation.

r003.rationale: The response does not propose reverting to gold-standard operation when the technology makes a mistake.
